title.en: Mantucalla and the Golden Sheep: The Yutip-Raymi Revels
title.zh: 曼圖卡利亞與金羊:太陽節歡宴

region.en: Mantucalla, royal resort near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近王室別苑曼圖卡利亞(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: At the first month's festival of the Sun the Inca retired with all his lords to Mantucalla to drink and enjoy the taqui called Huallina, a dance with singing performed four times in the day by the Yncas alone, while the mama-cunas, women of the Sun, gave them drink. At this festival were brought out the two female figures Pallasillu and Ynca-uillu, clothed in rich dress and plates of gold, and great figures of sheep, two of gold and two of silver, carried on litters by principal lords - in memory, they say, of the sheep which came forth from the tambo with them.
summary.zh: 歲首太陽節,印加王與眾卿退居曼圖卡利亞,飲宴作樂,行「瓦利納」歌舞,一日四遍,唯印加貴族可舞,太陽貞女(瑪瑪庫納)奉酒。節慶中抬出帕拉西略與印加威略二女神像,遍飾金片;又抬兩尊金羊、兩尊銀羊,由貴族以轎抬行——據說是為紀念當年隨始祖一同走出坦波驛站的羊群。

sensitivity.note: Festival description from Molina's month calendar; the golden sheep commemorate the ancestral llama figures of the founding episode.

passages.text: The Ynca, with all his lords, went to Mantucalla, and there remained to drink and enjoy himself in revelry and taquis. They called this taqui Huallina, and it was a dance with singing which was performed four times in the day. The Yncas alone celebrated this feast; and the mama-cunas, women of the Sun, gave drink to those who performed it; their own wives did not enter the place where the Yncas were, but remained outside in a court. All the vases and utensils from which they ate and drank, and with which they cooked the food, were of gold.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of Hauca (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: At this festival they brought out the two female figures called Pallasillu and Ynca-uillu, covered with very rich clothes and small plates of gold. In front they bore the suntur-paucar and certain great figures of the size of sheep, two of gold and two of silver, with cloths placed over the loins in the fashion of horse cloths. They were carried on litters, and this was done in memory of the sheep which, they say, came forth from the tambo with them. The Indians who carried them were principal lords dressed in very rich clothes, and they call the figures of gold and silver sheep corinapa collque-napa.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of Hauca (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Yahuayra: The Sowing Fast and the Prayer for a Prosperous Year
title.zh: 亞瓦伊拉:播種齋戒與豐年祈禱

region.zh: 庫斯科利馬潘帕(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In July, the sowing month, the people celebrated the festival called yahuayra, named from the song in which they besought the Creator for a full harvest. The Tarpuntaes fasted from the time the maize was sown until it stood a finger's length out of the ground, as did their wives and children, eating only boiled maize and herbs, drinking only the muddy concho, and chewing no coca. In red shirts to the feet, without mantles, they sang and danced at Limapampa, where the priests of the Creator sacrificed a white sheep, maize, coca, coloured plumes and mullu shells, praying that he who made all things out of nothing would grant a prosperous year; the priests of the Sun prayed for warmth and the Thunder, Chuqui Yllapa, for waters without hail.
summary.zh: 七月為播種之月,民眾慶祝「亞瓦伊拉」節,以所唱祈豐之歌為名。塔爾蓬泰祭司自播種之日起齋戒,直至玉米長出一指之高;其妻兒同齋,僅食煮玉米與野菜,不飲奇恰酒,只喝渾濁的孔喬,不嚼古柯。眾人身著及地紅衣、不披斗篷,在利馬潘帕唱歌起舞。造物主之祭司於清晨獻白羊、玉米、古柯、彩色羽飾與穆盧貝殼,祈求那位「從無中造出萬物」的主賜予豐年;太陽祭司祈日光暖育莊稼,雷神楚基伊亞帕降雨而不降雹。

sensitivity.note: Agricultural festival description; tagged with ritual-origin as a festival-calendar story.

passages.text: They called the month of July Moronpassa tarpuiquilla, and in it they celebrated the festivals called yahuayra, when they besought the Creator to grant them a full harvest in that year, for this was the month for sowing the seeds. The Tarpuntaes, who are a sort of priests, were careful to fast from the time the maize was sown until it was a finger's length out of the ground. Their wives and children also fasted, eating nothing during that time but boiled maize and herbs. They drank no chicha, but only muddy stuff called concho, and they chewed no coca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of July (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: All the common people celebrated a feast called yahuayra, from the name of the song they chaunted in which they besought the Creator to grant them a prosperous year. They sang it dressed in red shirts reaching to the feet, and no mantles. Then they came out to sing and dance in the place now called by the Spaniards Limapampa. Here the Priests of the Creator sacrificed a white sheep, maize, coca, plumes of coloured feathers, and sea shells called mullu, in the morning; beseeching the Creator to grant a prosperous year, and that, as He had made all things out of nothing and given them being, so He would be pleased to comply with their prayer.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of July (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Priests of the Sun, called Tarpuntaes, and the Priests of the Thunder also offered up sacrifices, praying the Sun to give warmth that so their food might be produced, and the Thunder, called Chuqui Yllapa, to send its waters to assist in the production, and not to bring down hail. As soon as the sacrifices were completed, the labourers went to their work, and the nobles to the house of the lord Ynca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of July (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Situa: Four Hundred Lances Drive the Evils to the Sea
title.zh: 淨疾節:四百長矛驅逐疫惡入海

region.zh: 庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In Coya-raymi, when the first rains brought sickness, the figures of the huacas were brought to Cuzco from Quito to Chile. Strangers, the broken-eared, the deformed and even the dogs were driven from the city, for their misfortune might drive away good fortune; then four hundred armed men, a hundred facing each of the four suyus, cried 'O sicknesses, disasters, misfortunes and dangers, go forth from the land', and relay-ran the shout along the four roads to the great rivers - the Apurimac, the river at Pisac, the river of Cusipampa - where the runners bathed themselves and their arms, so that the rivers of great volume would carry the evils away to the sea. All the people, great and small, shook their mantles at their doors crying 'Let the evils be gone', bathed at dawn, and played with burning straw torches called pancurcu.
summary.zh: 科亞雷米月(八月),初雨帶來疾病。各地瓦卡神像自基多至智利匯聚庫斯科。外人、耳裂者、畸形者乃至狗都被驅出城,因為厄運會趕走好運。四百名武裝男子在廣場集合,每百人面向一個蘇尤,高呼「疫病、災禍、不幸與危險,滾出此地!」隨後分四路接力奔跑傳喊,一路傳至阿普里馬克河等大河,傳喊者在河中沐浴並洗武器——大河終將把疫惡帶入大海。全城大小人民在門口抖動斗篷高呼「疫惡速去」,黎明赴河泉沐浴,再以點燃的草把(潘庫爾庫)互相拋擲嬉戲。

sensitivity.note: The great purification rite of Coya Raymi; its exclusion of the deformed is recorded here critically, as Molina preserves it.

passages.text: The month of August was called Coya-raymi, and in it they celebrated the Situa. To perform its ceremonies they brought the figures of their huacas from all parts of the land, from Quito to Chile, and placed them in the houses they had in Cuzco. The reason for celebrating the feast in this month was because the rains commenced, and with the first rains there was generally much sickness. They besought the Creator that during the year he would be pleased to shield them from sickness, as well in Cuzco as throughout the territory conquered by the Yncas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: First, all strangers, all whose ears were broken, and all deformed persons were sent out of the city, it being said that they should take no part in the ceremony, because they were in that state as a punishment for some fault; unfortunate people ought not to be present, because their ill-luck might drive away some piece of good fortune. They also drove out the dogs, that they might not howl. Then the people, armed as if for war, went to the square of Cuzco, crying out: 'O sicknesses, disasters, misfortunes, and dangers, go forth from the land.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Four hundred men of war assembled in the middle of the square where stood the urn of gold used at the sacrifice of chicha: one hundred faced towards Colla-suyu, one hundred to the westward towards Chincha-suyu, another hundred towards Anti-suyu, and the last hundred towards the south. They cried 'Go forth all evils', and each party set out at great speed along its appointed road, handing the cries on from lineage to mitimaes and from mitimaes to mitimaes, until at the great rivers - the Apurimac, the river at Pisac, the river at Quiquisana, the river of Cusipampa - they bathed themselves and washed their clothes and arms.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Their reason for bathing in these rivers was because they were rivers of great volume, and were supposed to empty themselves into the sea, and to carry the evils with them. When the ceremony commenced in Cuzco, all the people, great and small, came to their doors, crying out, shaking their mantles and llicllas, and shouting, 'Let the evils be gone. How greatly desired has this festival been by us. O Creator of all things, permit us to reach another year, that we may see another feast like this.' They all danced, including the Ynca, and in the morning twilight they went to the rivers and fountains to bathe, saying that their maladies would come out of them. Having finished bathing, they took great torches of straw, bound round with cords, which they lighted and continued to play with, passing them from one to the other; they called these torches pancurcu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Blood-Sprinkled Sancu and the Oath of the Four Suyus
title.zh: 血灑桑庫與四蘇尤之誓

region.zh: 庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: After the sacrifice of four unblemished unshorn sheep - one each to the Creator, the Thunder, the Sun and Huanacauri - the high priest sprinkled sancu pudding with their blood on plates of gold and warned the multitude: whoever eats the sancu in sin, with a double heart, is seen by the Sun their father, who will punish him with grievous troubles; but who eats with a single heart will be granted children and happy years. All rose, vowing never to murmur against the Creator, the Sun or the Thunder, and never to be traitors to the lord Inca; the priest took three fingers' worth, and all partook down to the little children, keeping no particle from falling to the ground - a great sin - and reserving portions for the absent and the sick. The lungs of the sacrificed sheep were inflated and read for the signs of the coming year.
summary.zh: 獻祭四隻無瑕未剪毛之羊(分別敬造物主、雷神、太陽、瓦納考里)後,大祭司以羊血灑金盤中的桑庫糊,向眾人宣告:凡心懷二意、帶罪而食者,太陽之父看得見,必降重災;凡誠心而食者,太陽與雷神必賜子嗣、豐年與所求之一切。全體起立立誓:絕不對造物主、太陽、雷神生怨,絕不背叛印加王,違者自領災殃。祭司取三指之量入口,眾人依次同食,直至孩童;為遠行者與病榻者留份,任何一粒落地都是大罪。祭畢,剖出羊肺吹脹,察其紋路以斷來年吉凶。

sensitivity.note: Oath rite preserved by Molina; demonstrates the fusion of kingship loyalty and solar cult.

passages.text: The Ynca and the people brought with them a very great quantity of flocks from all the four quarters... more than one hundred thousand, and it was necessary that all should be without spot or blemish, and with fleeces that had never been shorn. Presently the priest of the Sun selected four of the most perfect, and sacrificed them in the following order: one was offered to the Creator, another to the Thunder, another to the Sun, and another to Huanacauri. When this sacrifice was offered up, the priest had the sancu on great plates of gold, and he sprinkled it with the blood of the sheep.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The high priest then said in a loud voice so that all might hear: 'Take heed how you eat this sancu; for he who eats it in sin, and with a double will and heart, is seen by our father the Sun, who will punish him with grievous troubles. But he who with a single heart partakes of it, to him the Sun and the Thunder will show favour, and will grant children and happy years, and abundance, and all that he requires.' Then they all rose up to partake, first making a solemn vow before eating the yahuar-sancu, in which they promised never to murmur against the Creator, the Sun, or the Thunder; never to be traitors to their lord the Ynca, on pain of receiving condemnation and trouble.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The priest of the Sun took what he could hold on three fingers, put it into his mouth, and returned to his seat; and in this order all the tribes rose up and partook, down to the little children. They kept some of the yahuar-sancu for those who were absent, and sent some to those who were confined to their beds by sickness; they took it with such care that no particle was allowed to fall to the ground, this being looked upon as a great sin. When they killed the sacrificial sheep, they took out the lungs and inflated them, and the priests judged, from certain signs on them, whether all things would turn out prosperously in the coming year or not.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Prayers of the Situa: Creator, Sun, Thunder, Huacas
title.zh: 淨疾節禱文:造物主、太陽、雷與瓦卡

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Molina preserves the Quechua liturgy of the festival with Markham's translations: the prayer to the conquering, incomprehensible Creator who says 'let this be a man, let this be a woman' and dwells in the heights of heaven, in the thunder and the storm clouds; the prayer for fruitful flocks; the prayer to the huacas - Chanca-Uiracocha of Chuqui-chaca, Atun-Uiracocha of Urcos with its carved eagle and falcon, Apotin-Uiracocha of Amaybamba; the prayer that men be kept from hunger and the fruits from frost; the prayer to the Sun who said 'let there be day and night'; the prayer for the Inca that he may always be a conqueror, and for all the Incas that 'there may be Cuzcos and Tampus'; and the prayer to the sacred huacas, ancestors and grandsires, to bring their sons near to the Creator.
summary.zh: 莫利納保存了節慶的克丘亞禱文(馬卡姆英譯):向無可比擬、戰無不勝的造物主祈禱——祂說「使此人為男、使彼人為女」,居於高天、雷聲與風暴雲中;祈求羊群繁衍;向瓦卡祈禱——楚基查卡的昌卡-維拉科查、烏爾科斯的大維拉科查(廟門刻有鷹與隼)、阿馬伊班巴的阿波廷-維拉科查;祈求人民免於飢餓、五穀免於霜凍;向「說要有晝夜」的太陽祈禱;為印加王祈禱,願他常勝不敗;為歷代印加祈禱,「願庫斯科與坦波永存」;並向神聖瓦卡——祖先、先人們祈禱,求他們引子孫近於造物主。

sensitivity.note: Liturgical prayers are treated as religious records of the Quechua cult; marked 'religious' as canonical liturgy of the tradition.

passages.text: O Creator! [O conquering Uiracocha! Ever present Uiracocha!] Thou who art without equal unto the ends of the earth! Thou who givest life and strength to mankind, saying, let this be a man and let this be a woman: and as thou sayest, so thou givest life, and vouchsafest that men shall live in health and peace, and free from danger. Thou who dwellest in the heights of heaven, in the thunder, and in the storm clouds, hear us! and grant us eternal life. Have us in thy keeping, and receive this our offering, as it shall please thee, O Creator!
passages.note: Quechua prayer in Markham's 1873 translation (public domain), condensed; the liturgy is quoted as an archival religious text.

passages.text: O Creator! who doest wonders and marvels. O most merciful and almighty Creator! multiply our flocks and cause them to bring forth young, let the land continue in peace and free from danger, and these whom thou hast made, hold them in thy hand. ... O Creator! Thou who gavest being to the Sun, and afterwards said let there be day and night. Raise it and cause it to shine, and preserve that which thou hast created, that it may give light to men. O Sun! Thou who art in peace and safety, shine upon us, keep us from sickness, and keep us in health and safety.
passages.note: Quechua prayers in Markham's 1873 translation (public domain), condensed.

passages.text: O pious Creator, who ordered and saw fit that there should be a Lord Ynca, grant to the Ynca that he may be kept in peace, with his servants and vassals, that he may obtain the victory over his enemies and always be a conqueror. Cut not short his days, nor the days of his children, and give them peace, O Creator! ... O Sun! Thou who hast said, let there be Cuzcos and Tampus, grant that these thy children may conquer all other people. We beseech thee that thy children the Yncas may be conquerors always, for this hast thou created them.
passages.note: Quechua prayers in Markham's 1873 translation (public domain), condensed.

passages.text: O sacred Huacas, ancestors, grandsires, and parents! O Hatun-apu! O Apu Allastu! bring us near to the Creator, us thy sons, and our children, that they may be fortunate and near the Creator, as thou art. Chanca-Uiracocha was a huaca in Chuqui-chaca; Atun-Uiracocha is in the huaca of Urcos, where there was an eagle and a falcon carved in stone at the entrance of the huaca, and an image of a man with a white robe reaching to his feet; Apotin-Uiracocha is in Amaybamba, beyond Tampu.
passages.note: Quechua prayer and huaca notes in Markham's 1873 translation (public domain), condensed.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Lords of Gold Benches: Mummies in the Great Square
title.zh: 金座之主:大廣場上的王木乃伊

region.zh: 庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: During the Situa the embalmed bodies of dead lords and ladies were brought out, each by a person of the same lineage who had charge of it, washed in the baths which belonged to them when they were alive, warmed with the coarse sancu pudding, and set before them the food they had been most fond of when alive, which their keepers afterwards consumed. The image of the Sun called Apupunchau, the principal image of the temple, was set on a bench of gold in the square, with the images of the Creator and of the Thunder Chuqui-ylla each on its golden bench, the woman Coya-facssa dedicated to the Sun attending; the embalmed lords were deposited in the square on seats of gold in the order in which they had lived, Hanan-Cuzcos on one side and Hurin-Cuzcos on the other, and the whole city passed the day in eating and drinking.
summary.zh: 淨疾節中,先王王后的木乃伊由各世系專管之人抬出,放入其生前專用的浴池洗浴,以粗桑庫糊暖身,並在其前擺上生前最愛的食物,由看管者代食。太陽主像「阿普蓬喬」與造物主像、雷神楚基伊亞像各安金座於廣場,獻身太陽的科亞神女在旁侍立;歷代木乃伊按生前位次安放於金座,哈南庫斯科世系居一側,烏林庫斯科世系居另一側,全城飲宴終日。

sensitivity.note: Royal ancestor cult described by Molina; the mummies are treated as still-living lords, a central Andean belief.

passages.text: They also brought out the bodies of the dead lords and ladies which were embalmed, each one being brought out by the person of the same lineage who had charge of it. During the night these bodies were washed in the baths which belonged to them when they were alive. They were then brought back to their houses, and warmed with the same coarse pudding called sancu; and the food they had been most fond of when they were alive was placed before them, and afterwards the persons who were in charge of the bodies consumed the food.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: There also came forth the woman called Coya-facssa, who was dedicated to the Sun; she was either the sister or the daughter of the ruler. The priests carried the image of the Sun and placed it on a bench prepared for it in the square; the priests of the Creator likewise brought forth his image, and so did the priests of the Thunder, called Chuqui-ylla. Each had its bench of gold, and before them were borne yauris, made like sceptres of gold. At this feast they brought out all the embalmed bodies of their lords and ladies, very richly adorned; the bodies were carried by the descendants of the respective lineages and were deposited in the square on seats of gold, according to the order in which they lived, the Hanan-Cuzcos on one side and the Hurin-Cuzcos on the other.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)
